definition: A technology that creates virtual boundaries around real-world locations, triggering actions when devices enter or exit these predefined geographic areas.
metaDescription: Learn about geofencing technology, how it tracks your location for targeted services, and the privacy implications of location-based boundaries.
simpleExplanation: Geofencing is like drawing invisible circles around places on a map. When your phone enters or leaves these circles, it can automatically trigger actions like sending notifications, showing ads, or recording your visit.
whyItMatters: Geofencing enables precise location tracking and can create detailed profiles of your daily movements, work locations, and personal habits. This data is valuable to advertisers and raises concerns about surveillance and privacy.
technicalDetail: Geofencing uses GPS, cellular towers, Wi-Fi, or Bluetooth beacons to determine device location within defined polygonal or circular boundaries. When boundary crossing is detected, APIs trigger predefined actions like push notifications, data collection, or service activation.

examples.explanation: A clothing store app sends you a discount coupon when you walk within 100 feet of their location, encouraging you to visit and make a purchase.
Your home's thermostat automatically adjusts temperature and lights turn on when your phone's location shows you're approaching your house.
An employee timekeeping app automatically clocks you in when you arrive at your office building and clocks you out when you leave the premises.
